813.title: The dumb ox
813.hook: Thomas Aquinas is so quiet classmates mock him; his teacher says this ox's bellow will fill the world
813.howItsDone: Catholics honor Thomas Aquinas as a saint and Doctor of the Church; his feast is kept in the Church's calendar, and his Summa Theologiae is studied in seminaries and Catholic universities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a psalm on Oxford's coat of arms, and schools that grew beside cathedrals. Your line was faith builds schools. What hard thing did you learn? Day eight hundred thirteen.

In the classroom there's a young friar who hardly ever speaks. He's big, slow-moving, from a noble Italian family, and he sits through every lecture and every argument in silence, taking it in. His classmates have a name for him. They call him the dumb ox. In their Latin, dumb meant mute, not stupid, but the joke cut both ways: a large animal that doesn't make a sound. One of them, feeling sorry for him, offers to help him with his lessons. The quiet friar says thank you, and lets him. His name is Thomas Aquinas. Today's word is his nickname: dumb ox.
screen: `A FRIAR WHO HARDLY SPEAKS.` → `THEY CALL HIM THE DUMB OX.` → `A CLASSMATE OFFERS TO HELP.`

segments.voice: First, the tutor. William of Tocco, who wrote an early life of Thomas, tells what happened next. The kind classmate began explaining a lesson, got lost halfway, and couldn't find his way out. Thomas, gently, picked up the thread and explained it clearly. The classmate asked him, from then on, to be the tutor. Then, the teacher. The master of that school was Albert, a Dominican scholar later called Albert the Great. Albert noticed the quiet one, and set him a hard question to argue in front of everyone. Thomas answered it so well that Albert turned to the room. The account gives his words like this: you call him the dumb ox, but one day his bellowing will be heard throughout the world. Next, the bellow. Thomas went on to teach at Paris and wrote the Summa Theologiae, laying out questions about God and the world in the disputation pattern from yesterday: question, objections, answer, reply. Catholics count him a Doctor of the Church, and his writing is still read in seminaries and universities. The ox did bellow. Last, the silence. It came first. Tradition remembers Thomas, even after he was known, as gentle in argument, slow to speak and careful with other people's views. The Douay-Rheims Ecclesiastes says there is "A time to keep silence, and a time to speak." For Thomas, the first time made the second one possible. The room underrated him because he wasn't loud. His teacher heard what the room missed: the ox will bellow.
screen: `THE TUTOR GETS LOST.` · `ALBERT SETS A HARD QUESTION.` · `THE SUMMA, AND A DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH.` · `THE SILENCE CAME FIRST.` · then, large: `A TIME TO KEEP SILENCE, AND A TIME TO SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect a quiet person. Choose one: a colleague who rarely speaks up, a relative at the end of the table, a child who watches more than talks. Think of what you actually know about what goes on in them. Maybe less than it seems. Hold them in mind kindly for the sit, and wonder what they've noticed that the loud people missed. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If not, simply resolve to ask them a real question soon, and wait for the answer. The bell holds the time.
Dumb ox. The nickname classmates gave the silent young Thomas Aquinas, until his teacher Albert said his bellowing would be heard throughout the world. Today's word.
Your line: the ox will bellow. Today, in one meeting or meal, turn to the quietest person there and ask what they think. Then really listen. Day eight hundred thirteen.

814.title: Bonaventure's journey
814.hook: a Franciscan maps the mind's road to God, starting from creatures
814.howItsDone: Franciscans read Bonaventure's Journey of the Mind into God as a guide to prayer, and Catholics honor him as a saint and Doctor of the Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dumb ox, the silent Thomas Aquinas, and a teacher who heard what the room missed. Your line was the ox will bellow. Whose quiet answer did you wait for? Day eight hundred fourteen.

A footprint in wet sand. Nobody's there, but you can tell someone walked this way, which direction they went, maybe how fast. The print isn't the person. It points to the person. A Franciscan friar named Bonaventure, who led Francis's brothers, went up the mountain of La Verna to pray, and there, he says, he began to map the mind's way up to God. In that map the whole world is like the sand: covered in footprints, every creature a trace of the one who made it. He wrote it as a short book, step by step, from those traces up to God. Today's word is that road: Bonaventure's journey.
screen: `A FOOTPRINT IN WET SAND.` → `IT POINTS TO THE PERSON.` → `A WORLD COVERED IN TRACES.`

segments.voice: First, the book. Its Latin title is Itinerarium mentis in Deum: the mind's journey into God. Bonaventure says the plan came to him on La Verna, as he thought about the six-winged seraph that Francis saw there, and he builds the road as six steps, like six wings. Then, outside us. The first steps start with what you can see and touch. Bonaventure calls creatures vestigia, footprints. Their size, their beauty, their order all point back to their maker. He leans on Saint Paul, who in the Douay-Rheims writes: "For the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." A leaf, a river, a sparrow: not God, but a print that says God passed this way. Next, inside us. The middle steps turn inward. Your own mind, which remembers, understands and loves, Bonaventure calls an image of God, a mirror rather than a footprint. Look at how you know and love things, and you are looking at a likeness of the one who made you. Last, beyond. The final steps go past both. And here the map turns. At the top of the road, he says, don't ask for more learning but for grace, not for understanding but for desire, not for a teacher but for the bridegroom. The journey that began with careful study ends in prayer, in silence, in love. Francis praised brother sun; his follower drew a map from the same world. It runs through creatures to God.
screen: `SIX STEPS, LIKE SIX WINGS.` · `CREATURES ARE FOOTPRINTS.` · `THE MIND IS A MIRROR.` · `AT THE TOP: GRACE, NOT LEARNING.` · then, large: `CLEARLY SEEN, BY THE THINGS THAT ARE MADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for God in one creature, or, if that's not your language, look for what's beyond it. Choose one living thing near you, or one you can remember clearly: a weed in a crack of the sidewalk, a dog asleep, a bird you saw this morning. For the sit, look at it the way Bonaventure did. Its shape. Its order. The fact that it's here at all. Ask what it's a footprint of. Don't hurry toward an answer. If you pray, you can let the looking become thanks. The bell holds the time.
Bonaventure's journey. The Franciscan map of the mind's road to God, from creatures as footprints, to the mind as a mirror, to grace beyond them both. Today's word.
Your line: through creatures to God. Today, stop once at something living, and ask whose footprint it is. Day eight hundred fourteen.

pairs: an image of God, a mirror

sources.ref: Romans 1:20

815.title: Elizabeth of Hungary (1207–1231)
815.hook: a princess who built a hospital and served in it, widowed young
815.howItsDone: Catholics honor Elizabeth of Hungary as a patron of hospitals, nurses and the Secular Franciscans, and hospitals, parishes and charities bear her name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bonaventure's map, with creatures as footprints. Your line was through creatures to God. Whose footprint did you stop at? Day eight hundred fifteen.

A young woman is walking down the steep path from a castle, her cloak gathered in front of her, heavy with something. Someone stops her and asks what she's carrying. She opens the cloak. Roses. In the common telling, she was carrying bread to the poor, and it turned to roses so she wouldn't be caught. It's on altarpieces and stained glass, and statues give her an apron full of flowers. The woman is a princess, a king's daughter married into a German court. Her name is Elizabeth. Today's word is Elizabeth.
screen: `A CLOAK HEAVY WITH SOMETHING.` → `SHE OPENS IT: ROSES.` → `A KING'S DAUGHTER.`

segments.voice: First, the legend. The roses come from later tellings, and the details shift: sometimes it's her husband who stops her, sometimes someone else. The women who served her, who later gave testimony about her life, don't tell it. So what did they tell? Then, the bread. They describe a princess who would not stay in the castle. In a time of hunger she gave out grain from the family stores. She had a hospital built below the castle and went down to it herself, feeding the sick and the poor with her own hands, washing them, carrying the children. Her husband Ludwig, the story goes, loved her and let her do it. Next, the loss. Ludwig set out with a crusade and died of sickness on the way, and Elizabeth was widowed young, with small children. Her life at court fell apart. She left, poor, and in the end settled at Marburg, where she built another hospital and served in it, wearing a plain gray habit. Tradition links her to the Franciscans, whose way of poverty had reached Germany from Assisi. She died young. Last, why the roses stuck. The witnesses never needed a miracle to describe her. Jesus's words in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims, describe her days well enough: "For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink." The legend turns that into a picture. Whatever was in her apron, people remembered that she carried it down the hill herself. The Church named her a saint, and hospitals and charities still carry her name. Roses in her apron.
screen: `THE ROSES COME FROM LATER TELLINGS.` · `A HOSPITAL BELOW THE CASTLE.` · `WIDOWED, POOR, STILL SERVING.` · `I WAS HUNGRY, AND YOU GAVE ME TO EAT.` · then, large: `SHE CARRIED IT HERSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve with your own hands, starting with a plan. For the sit, think of one concrete act of service you could do in person this week, not by sending money or a link. Cooking for someone. Visiting. Cleaning a neighbor's step. Driving someone to an appointment. Choose one. Then picture your own hands doing it: what you'll carry, where you'll walk. If you pray, you can offer the task to God before you do it. The bell holds the time.
Elizabeth. A king's daughter who built hospitals and served in them herself, remembered in a legend of bread turned to roses. Today's word.
Your line: roses in her apron. Today, carry something to someone yourself, food, a note, a tool they need, instead of having it sent. Day eight hundred fifteen.

816.title: Louis IX
816.hook: a king who fed the poor at his table, and who also led crusades
816.carry: a king at table with the poor
816.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Louis, and parishes, cities and schools bear his name; the Church honors him for his faith and charity while historians, including Catholic ones, also examine his crusades and his laws.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elizabeth, a princess who carried the bread down the hill herself. Your line was roses in her apron. What did you carry by hand? Day eight hundred sixteen.

Would you rather be a leper, or commit a mortal sin? A king puts that question to his friend, with others listening. The friend, a knight named John of Joinville, answers honestly: he'd rather commit a great many sins than be a leper. The king says nothing in front of the others. Later, alone, he tells Joinville he has it backward: no sickness of the body is as ugly as a sin in the soul. Joinville wrote the whole thing down, years after, in a book about his friend. The king was Louis, king of France, whom the Church would call a saint. Today's word is Louis IX.
screen: `A LEPER, OR A MORTAL SIN?` → `AN HONEST ANSWER.` → `A KING CORRECTS HIM, ALONE.`

segments.voice: First, the table. Joinville describes a king who fed the poor, and often had poor men brought to eat where he was, sometimes serving them himself. Then, the feet. Louis once asked Joinville whether he washed the feet of the poor on Holy Thursday. Joinville was horrified: never, he said, the feet of those peasants. Louis told him that was a poor answer, since Christ had done it. Jesus's words in John, in the Douay-Rheims: "you also ought to wash one another's feet." Joinville also remembers Louis sitting under an oak tree at Vincennes, hearing anyone who came with a complaint, with no guard between them. Next, the other side. This same king led crusades. He was captured in Egypt, ransomed, and died on another crusade in North Africa. The crusades brought war and death to Christians, Muslims and others. And Louis's laws were harsh to the Jews of France; in his reign copies of the Talmud were burned in Paris. Catholic historians tell these things too. Last, holding both. The Church canonized Louis for his faith, his prayer and his charity, not for every decision he made. A saint, Catholics say, is someone in heaven, not someone without faults on earth. You can admire the king at the table and still name what his wars and laws cost. Today's line keeps the picture people remember: a king at table with the poor.
screen: `THE POOR AT THE KING'S TABLE.` · `WASH ONE ANOTHER'S FEET.` · `CRUSADES, AND HARSH LAWS.` · `ADMIRATION AND HONESTY TOGETHER.` · then, large: `YOU ALSO OUGHT TO WASH ONE ANOTHER'S FEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold admiration and honesty together. Choose someone you admire, living or dead, a parent, a teacher, a figure from history. For the sit, first let yourself see what's good in them, clearly. Then, without anger, let one real fault come into view as well. Don't cancel the good. Don't erase the fault. Just hold both in the same hand. If you pray, you can pray for them as they really were. The bell holds the time.
Louis IX. The king of France remembered as Saint Louis: a king who fed and served the poor, and who also led crusades. Today's word.
Your line: a king at table with the poor. Today, make room at your table, or at your lunch, for one person who usually eats alone. Day eight hundred sixteen.

washing the feet of the poor

817.title: The cathedrals
817.hook: built over generations by people who wouldn't see them finished
817.howItsDone: Each Catholic diocese has a cathedral where the bishop's chair stands; the bishop presides there at major celebrations, such as the Chrism Mass in Holy Week, and the anniversary of the cathedral's dedication is kept as a feast in the diocese.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Louis the Ninth, a king who fed the poor and also went to war, and we held both at once. Your line was a king at table with the poor. Who did you make room for? Day eight hundred seventeen.
screen: `A KING AT TABLE WITH THE POOR.`

segments.voice: A mason sets a block high in a wall, taps it level, and climbs down the scaffold. There is no roof above him yet. There is no tower. His son may lay the next row of stone, and his grandson may be the one who hears the first Mass under the finished vault. Some great churches rose this way, a few courses at a time, while the people who began them grew old and were buried in the churchyard beside the work. Today's word is the building they gave their lives to: the cathedral.
screen: `A STONE SET, NO ROOF ABOVE.` → `THE SON LAYS THE NEXT ROW.` → `THE GRANDSON HEARS THE MASS.`

segments.voice: Start with what makes a church a cathedral. It isn't size. A cathedral is the church that holds a bishop's chair, called the cathedra, the sign of his work of teaching and shepherding. A small church with that chair is a cathedral. An enormous church without it is not. So at the heart of the grandest building in town sits a piece of furniture, and a job. Next, the long build. A cathedral could outlast the people who started it. Masons, carpenters, glassmakers, donors who paid for one window or gave one season of labor. The building outlasts their names. Then, the reason. The Douay-Rheims psalm puts it in one line: "Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it." The psalm isn't about masonry, but people raised these churches as if the stonework itself could be offered, as if every block were laid for God before it was laid for a town. Finally, the posture. The letter to the Hebrews remembers the ancestors of faith who died still waiting, "not having received the promises, but beholding them afar off." That is the cathedral builder's stance. You lay a stone you will never stand under. You trust someone you will never meet to finish it. A cathedral is a long sentence, and each generation gets to write a few words of it.
screen: `A CATHEDRAL HOLDS A BISHOP'S CHAIR.` · `THE BUILD OUTLASTS THE BUILDERS.` · `UNLESS THE LORD BUILD THE HOUSE.` · `BEHOLDING THEM AFAR OFF.` · then, large: `BUILT FOR GRANDCHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lay one stone. Before the sit, choose something small you could begin that will outlast today. A seed in a pot. The first page of a notebook for someone younger. A jar for coins toward a cause you care about. A letter meant to be opened years from now. Name it. Then settle, and breathe slowly. Picture the person who might finish it, or simply be glad of it one day: a child, a grandchild, a stranger. If you pray, you can borrow the line from Hebrews, beholding them afar off. If you don't, just hold the face of whoever comes after you. The bell holds the time.
Cathedral. The church that holds a bishop's chair, sometimes raised by people who never saw it finished. Today's word.
Your line: built for grandchildren. Today, take the first small step on the thing you named, a seed, a page, a coin, and leave it for someone later to find. Day eight hundred seventeen.

a small church with a bishop's chair

818.title: Stained glass
818.hook: windows as a Bible for people who couldn't read
818.howItsDone: Catholic churches old and new use stained-glass windows to show scenes from scripture and the lives of the saints, and some parishes offer tours or guides that walk visitors through the stories window by window.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cathedrals, raised a few rows of stone at a time by people who never saw the roof. Your line was built for grandchildren. What did you start that someone else will finish? Day eight hundred eighteen.

What does a woman who can't read see when she walks into a medieval church on a bright morning? Not words. Color. A blue so deep it looks like night. A red like a coal in the hearth. And inside the color, people: a man asleep under a ladder of angels, a woman at a well, a baby in a manger, a body on a cross. As the sun moves across the sky, one window brightens, then the next, and the stories light up in turn. She can't read a page, but she can read the wall. Today's word is the glass that tells those stories: stained glass.
screen: `NO WORDS, ONLY COLOR.` → `PEOPLE INSIDE THE COLOR.` → `SHE CAN READ THE WALL.`

segments.voice: First, the reason for pictures. Pope Gregory the Great once wrote to a bishop who had smashed the images in his church, worried that people were worshiping them. Gregory told him he was right to forbid worship of images, and wrong to break them. What writing gives to those who can read, he said, a picture gives to the unlearned who look at it: in it they read what they cannot read in books. That's the idea behind calling the windows a Bible for people who couldn't read. Second, the way the story is told. A window is cut into panels, scene after scene, the way a comic strip is, so a life can be followed from one picture to the next. Third, the light itself. The Gospel of John says of Christ, in the Douay-Rheims: "That was the true light, which enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world." Glass makes no light of its own. It receives the sun, and gives it back in color, shaped into a story. A medieval abbot, Suger, who rebuilt the abbey church of Saint-Denis near Paris, wrote that beauty seen with the eyes could lead the mind up toward that true light. Finally, the thing that's easy to forget. From inside the church at night, a stained-glass window is dark. The lead lines are there, the colors are there, but the story waits. It only speaks when light comes through it.
screen: `PICTURES FOR THOSE WHO CAN'T READ.` · `A STORY TOLD PANEL BY PANEL.` · `THE TRUE LIGHT, GIVEN BACK IN COLOR.` · `DARK UNTIL THE SUN COMES THROUGH.` · then, large: `LIGHT THAT TELLS STORIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at light through glass. Find a window, a glass of water, a bottle, a jar held up toward a lamp. Settle where you can see the light pass through it. For the sit, just watch. Notice how the glass changes the light: bends it, colors it, throws it onto the table. Notice that the glass is doing nothing on its own. If you pray, you can hold John's line, the true light, which enlighteneth every man. If you don't, just let the light be the only thing happening for a while. The bell holds the time.
Stained glass. Colored glass set in lead, cut into panels that tell scripture and the saints' lives to anyone who can see, whether or not they can read. Today's word.
Your line: light that tells stories. Today, notice one moment when light through a window falls on something ordinary, and stop long enough to see what it shows you. Day eight hundred eighteen.

a story told scene by scene

what it means: a Bible in light, scripture and saints told panel by panel for people who couldn't read.
what a scholar hears: Gregory the Great's letter: what writing gives readers, a picture gives the unlearned who look at it.

819.title: The nuns of Helfta
819.hook: Gertrude and Mechthild, whose visions of Christ's heart prepared the Sacred Heart devotion
819.howItsDone: Catholics keep the Solemnity of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus each year, and some honor Saint Gertrude on her feast in November; images of the Sacred Heart hang in homes and churches, and some families enthrone one in the house.

segments.voice: Yesterday, stained glass, a Bible in color for people who couldn't read. Your line was light that tells stories. Where did the light land? Today ends the week. Day eight hundred nineteen.

At the Last Supper, the Gospel of John gives one small, close detail. In the Douay-Rheims: "Now there was leaning on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved." One disciple, head against the chest of Christ, near enough to hear his heart. Centuries later, in a convent in Saxony called Helfta, women sang that Gospel in choir and read it in their books, and some of them prayed their way into that very spot. Today we meet them: the nuns of Helfta.
screen: `LEANING ON JESUS' BOSOM.` → `NEAR ENOUGH TO HEAR HIS HEART.` → `A CONVENT CALLED HELFTA.`

segments.voice: Start with two women in one house. Mechthild of Hackeborn led the singing in the convent choir. Gertrude, remembered as Gertrude the Great, came to Helfta as a child and grew into a scholar of scripture. Both received visions, and their sisters helped write them down: Gertrude's in a book called the Herald of Divine Love, Mechthild's in the Book of Special Grace. Next, the heartbeat. In the Herald, on the feast of Saint John, Gertrude sees herself resting beside John at the Lord's breast, and she hears his heart beating. So she asks John a bold question: you heard this too, so why did you write nothing about it? In her account, John answers that the sweetness of those heartbeats was kept for later times, when the world had grown cold and would need warming. Then, the wound. John's Gospel says that at the cross, "one of the soldiers with a spear opened his side, and immediately there came out blood and water." For the women of Helfta, that opened side became a door: a way into the heart of Christ, a place to rest, to be known, to pray. Finally, what came after. Later Catholic devotion to the Sacred Heart grew around other visionaries, and some histories of that devotion begin here, with these singing, reading women and a heart they heard beating.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray with a hand on your heart. Sit comfortably and lay one hand flat on your chest. Wait until you can feel your own heartbeat, or just the rise and fall of breath under your palm. Stay with that rhythm. If you pray, you can borrow the words of Jesus in Matthew's Gospel, learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart, and let them ride on the beat. If you don't, simply keep listening to the one heart that has been beating for you all your life without being asked. The bell holds the time.
Helfta. The convent in Saxony where Gertrude and Mechthild wrote of visions that drew them close to the heart of Christ. Today's word.
